headline: Building a Document Q&A Bot: Embeddings Are Trickier Than They Look
summary: Developer shares experience building a Q&A bot for internal docs, highlights challenges with embeddings.
details: The developer spent a weekend building a Q&A bot for their team's internal documents, aiming to provide instant answers to frequently asked questions.
They used OpenAI embeddings, stored them in Pinecone, and used GPT-4 to generate answers from retrieved chunks, but faced challenges with naive chunking, chunk size, and overlap.
The developer ultimately landed on a hybrid approach that balances precision and context length, and advises starting with a simpler baseline and adding embeddings if necessary.
caption:
Trickier than they look? Building a Q&A bot with embeddings just got a lot more complicated.

The developer spent a weekend building a Q&A bot for their team's internal documents, aiming to provide instant answers to frequently asked questions.

They used OpenAI embeddings, stored them in Pinecone, and used GPT-4 to generate answers from retrieved chunks, but faced challenges with naive chunking, chunk size, and overlap.

The developer ultimately landed on a hybrid approach that balances precision and context length, and advises starting with a simpler baseline and adding embeddings if necessary.

headline: Hashing isn't encryption: DEV explains the crucial difference
summary: Hashing turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint, but it's not encryption. Understanding the difference is key to password security.
details: Hashing and encryption are often confused, but they serve different purposes. Hashing is a one-way process that turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint.
A hash function like SHA-256 produces a fixed-size output, regardless of the input size. This means that infinitely many possible inputs map to the same hash, making reversal impossible.
The real mistake happens when using general-purpose hashes like SHA-256 for password storage. These hashes are designed to be fast, which makes them vulnerable to guessing attacks.
Two defenses can close this gap: using purpose-built slow hashes like Argon2 or bcrypt with a per-user salt, and helping users pick strong, unique passwords.
caption:
Did you know hashing isn't encryption? Learn the crucial difference.

Hashing and encryption are often confused, but they serve different purposes. Hashing is a one-way process that turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint.

A hash function like SHA-256 produces a fixed-size output, regardless of the input size. This means that infinitely many possible inputs map to the same hash, making reversal impossible.

The real mistake happens when using general-purpose hashes like SHA-256 for password storage. These hashes are designed to be fast, which makes them vulnerable to guessing attacks.

Two defenses can close this gap: using purpose-built slow hashes like Argon2 or bcrypt with a per-user salt, and helping users pick strong, unique passwords.
